context: attached low-rise unit · party-wall & shared-services coordination

brief.intro: New to this project type? A townhouse is a low-rise dwelling built in a row, sharing at least one party wall with its neighbour. The building itself is simple — two or three storeys, straightforward structure — so the programme is dominated by the finishing trade sequence rather than by engineering complexity. What makes a townhouse different from a standalone house is coordination along the terrace: party-wall structure, fire/acoustic separation and shared services routes must be resolved before finishing can proceed unit by unit. Units are usually built and released as a rolling row rather than one at a time, so a delay in one unit's blockwork or waterproofing can hold up its neighbour sharing the same wall or roofline. As with any residential type, wet areas — bathrooms and kitchens — set the pace: nothing progresses past them until waterproofing is tested and released.

scope.desc: Blockwork/frame, party-wall fire & acoustic separation, floor slabs and roof structure per unit.

scope.name: Roof & external envelope
scope.desc: Roof waterproofing, external render/cladding and terrace/balcony waterproofing.

scope.name: MEP first fix
scope.desc: Plumbing, electrical and light HVAC rough-in through walls and slab, coordinated across the party wall.

scope.name: Wet-area waterproofing
scope.desc: Bathroom/kitchen tanking and leak testing before tiling can start.

scope.name: Screed & tiling
scope.desc: Floor screed and wall/floor tiling to wet areas and living spaces.

scope.name: MEP second fix
scope.desc: Sanitary fixtures, switches/sockets, light fittings and AC units.

scope.name: Painting & joinery
scope.desc: Internal paint, doors, wardrobes and kitchen units.

scope.name: Snagging & handover
scope.desc: Per-unit inspection and handover, typically staggered along the row.

must_get_right: Resolve party-wall separation (fire & acoustic) before either side's finishing starts — it's a shared interface, not one contractor's problem.
Protect the wet-area waterproofing test — nothing downstream (tiling, second fix) should start until it's tested and released.
Plan the row as a rolling wave, not independent units — a stuck unit can block its neighbour's shared wall or roofline.
Coordinate shared services routes that cross the party line — risers, roof drainage — early, before both sides close up.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. A typical-unit fragnet is built once and repeated along the terrace with a rolling offset between units.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard 6-day working week. Wet-area waterproofing curing and test time is built into the calendar as real non-working duration — it is never compressed to protect a date.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs structure & party-wall closure → roof waterproofing → MEP first fix → wet-area tanking & test → tiling → second fix → snagging → handover. Because units share a wall and roofline, the row's slowest unit sets the pace for its neighbours either side.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and finishes schedule frozen per unit type before release; party-wall design resolved before either side starts blockwork; a single continuous mobilisation along the row.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Shared scaffolding and access along the terrace; limited laydown space between units; finishing-trade crews shared across the row are the main resource constraint on the wave rate.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: party-wall interface rework, wet-area test failures pushing tiling, and weather delaying external render. Contingency is held ahead of wet-area testing and before row handover rather than spread across individual units.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (row/phase handover milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to per-unit Level 4 for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
